title: Measuring Colorimetric Properties of Loess-Paleosol Sequences
author: Laag, Lagroix, et al.

steps.title: Calculate second derivative and TBA for goethite
steps.instruction: Transform each DRS reflectance spectrum to Kubelka‑Munk absorbance, compute its second derivative, locate the first minimum between 410 nm and 430 nm and the subsequent maximum between 440 nm and 460 nm, then calculate the absolute difference of these two points (the true band amplitude, TBA) as the semi‑quantitative goethite amount for each of the five individual measurements of the sediment sample.

substeps.instruction: Calculate the second derivative of the KM‑absorbance spectrum.
Identify the first minimum in the 410‑430 nm interval.
Identify the maximum in the 440‑460 nm interval.
Compute the absolute difference between the minimum and maximum (TBA).

steps.title: Calculate second derivative and TBA for hematite
steps.instruction: Using the same second‑derivative procedure, find the minimum between 510 nm and 530 nm and the maximum between 550 nm and 580 nm, and calculate their absolute difference as the hematite true band amplitude for each of the five measurements per sample.

substeps.instruction: From the second‑derivative KM‑absorbance spectrum, locate the minimum in the 510‑530 nm range.
Locate the maximum in the 550‑580 nm range.
Calculate the absolute difference (TBA) to represent semi‑quantitative hematite content.

steps.title: Acquire FTIR spectra of samples
steps.instruction: Measure each sample on a Bruker Vector 22 FTIR spectrometer equipped with an ATR diamond crystal, collecting an average of 64 scans over the wavenumber range 4000 cm⁻¹ to 400 cm⁻¹ at a resolution of 8 cm⁻¹.

substeps.instruction: Mount the sample on the ATR diamond crystal.
Set the spectrometer to acquire 64 scans (average).
Define the spectral range from 4000 cm⁻¹ to 400 cm⁻¹.
Set the spectral resolution to 8 cm⁻¹.
Run the acquisition and save the spectrum.

steps.title: Extract goethite and calcite band amplitudes
steps.instruction: From each ATR‑FTIR spectrum, determine the minima and maxima surrounding the target wavenumbers, use the band near 450 cm⁻¹ for goethite and the band near 1428 cm⁻¹ (allowing a ±11 cm⁻¹ deviation) for calcite, and calculate the mean signal value between the identified minimum and maximum as the absolute band amplitude for each mineral.

substeps.instruction: Identify the minimum and maximum absorbance around 450 cm⁻¹ (goethite).
Identify the minimum and maximum absorbance around 1428 cm⁻¹, accepting positions from 1417 cm⁻¹ to 1439 cm⁻¹ (calcite).
Compute the mean of the absorbance values between each pair of extrema to obtain the goethite and calcite band amplitudes.

description: Mid-infrared spectrometry, capable of tracking goethite and calcite concentrations semi-quantitatively, was measured on a subset of 719 samples from the SK18 LPS using a Fourier Transform Infrared (FTIR) Brucker Vector 22 spectrometer equipped with an Attenuated Total Reflection (ATR) sampling accessory and diamond crystal. The samples (mean of 64 scans) were scanned from 4000 cm−1 to 400 cm−1 at an 8 cm−1 resolution. Using the substation between minima and maxima of wavenumber absorbance, two band peak values were selected to calculate the mean signal value for calcite and goethite. Wavenumbers were selected after [24] for goethite (450 cm−1) and [25] for calcite (1428 cm−1). For calcite, note that the laser beam activates the stretching mode of CO3 in an asymmetrical behavior [26]. This causes a strong peak in the absorbance spectrum calculated from the ATR-FTIR measured spectra. However, the resulting peak wavenumber-position at 1428 cm−1 is experimentally considered and is accompanied by a standard deviation of ± 11 cm−1. We tried to circumvent this possible deviation from a fixed wavenumber position by applying ranges of the absorbance signal's minimum- and maximum wavenumber position per sample, allowing for a standard deviation that does not influence the calculated absolute band amplitude. The ATR-FTIR semi-quantitative concentrations for goethite and calcite were compared to the corrected box DRS goethite TBA and luminance L* values. Calcite (in primary and/or secondary form) is a very bright, nearly white mineral, which clearly influences the overall luminance (L*). Previous LPS studies, e.g., [20], have demonstrated calcite content to correlate well to L*. Moreover, during field sampling of SK18 LPS, we conducted systematical tests with low-concentrated HCl at each sampling depth and attested to the occurrence of carbonates (see supplementary Table 1S of [12]). Therefore, DRS-derived L* values are considered here to proxy for calcite concentration. Fig. 6
